outline.chapter_title: Background, Platform Mechanics, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: Sets the stage with the facts, the Cameo transactions that generated the videos, how Jimmy Kimmel used them on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and how the case reached the Second Circuit. Explains what materials the courts could consider on a motion to dismiss and the standard of review.
subtopics: Parties and roles: George Santos (plaintiff–copyright owner), Jimmy Kimmel, ABC, and The Walt Disney Company
How Cameo works and Kimmel’s pseudonymous requests for personalized paid videos
JKL’s “Will Santos Say It?” segments using the resulting videos for mockery/commentary
Santos’s registrations in the videos and their publication timing
Claims asserted: federal copyright infringement; state-law breach of contract, breach of implied contract, and fraudulent inducement
District Court ruling: Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal based on fair use and failure of state-law claims (with preemption noted below)
Appellate review: de novo review of 12(b)(6) dismissal; consideration of the complaint, incorporated materials, and judicial notice of Copyright Office records

outline.chapter_title: Fair Use Framework and Procedural Gatekeeping
outline.description: Introduces the statutory fair use doctrine and the Second Circuit’s approach to assessing it, including when courts may resolve fair use at the pleading stage. Highlights the centrality of the transformative-use inquiry and the objective ‘reasonable observer’ perspective, and clarifies the limited role of alleged bad faith.
subtopics: Fair use as an affirmative defense designed to avoid rigid application that would chill creativity
The four nonexclusive statutory factors under 17 U.S.C. § 107
Transformative use: focus on new purpose or character as judged by a reasonable observer
Pleading-stage adjudication: when fair use can be decided on a motion to dismiss by comparing the works and the complaint
Alleged deception or bad faith after Harper & Row: why it does not, by itself, defeat otherwise fair commentary or criticism

outline.chapter_title: Applying the Fair Use Factors to Santos’s Videos and JKL
outline.description: Walks through the Second Circuit’s factor-by-factor analysis. Explains why the first factor strongly favored Kimmel, how publication status and market-substitution principles informed the remaining factors, and why the court could resolve fair use using only the works and the pleadings.
subtopics: Factor 1 (purpose and character): JKL’s new purpose—commenting on Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money—was different from the videos’ original uplifting messages
Rejecting the ‘instigator’ argument: even if Kimmel prompted the content, the inquiry is objective; subjective purposes of either party are not controlling
Bad faith contention: pseudonymous requests did not show an intent to supplant Santos’s market; the use was for sarcastic criticism/commentary
Factor 2 (nature of the work): the videos were published the day they were created; publication status weakens any claim to heightened protection for unpublished works
Factor 3 (amount and substantiality): commentary and criticism may require extensive copying; the use was tied to the critical purpose
Factor 4 (market effect): no usurpation of Santos’s market; criticism/lampooning is not a cognizable licensing market to be protected; the segments were not substitutes for Cameo videos
Bottom line: comparing the videos and the JKL segments sufficed to find fair use on the pleadings

outline.chapter_title: Contract-Based State Claims: Third-Party Beneficiary and Implied Contract Theories
outline.description: Explains why the contract theories failed regardless of Copyright Act preemption. Distinguishes the Illinois-law third-party-beneficiary claim under Cameo’s Terms of Service from the New York-law implied-in-fact contract claim and details the pleading gaps.
subtopics: Preemption posture: court declines to decide; resolves on failure to state a claim
Direct breach claim under Cameo Terms (Illinois law): strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries; requires an intent ‘practically an express declaration’ to benefit nonparties
No express third-party-beneficiary language conferring enforcement rights on Santos; contrast with provisions that do expressly benefit third parties
Implied-in-fact contract (New York law): must plead essential terms and a meeting of the minds
Complaint’s deficiencies: no specific nonconclusory terms or plausible assent that Kimmel agreed to abide by Cameo’s Terms

outline.chapter_title: Fraudulent Inducement and the Out-of-Pocket Rule
outline.description: Analyzes why the fraudulent inducement claim failed under New York law. Focuses on the damages element—actual pecuniary loss—and how Santos’s pleadings did not satisfy it.
subtopics: Damages requirement: New York’s out-of-pocket rule for fraud
What counts as out-of-pocket loss versus what does not (e.g., reputational harm or loss of expected profits)
Application to these facts: no actual monetary loss alleged from making or delivering the videos
Result: dismissal for failure to plead legally cognizable fraud damages

outline.description: Synthesizes the outcomes on all claims and extracts practical lessons. Highlights the opinion’s guidance on transformative commentary, the narrow role of alleged deception in fair use, and the need for precise pleading in contract and fraud claims.
subtopics: Disposition: Affirmance of dismissal—copyright claims barred by fair use; state-law claims fail to state a claim
Key fair use lessons: objective assessment of purpose; commentary and criticism can be strongly transformative; fair use can be resolved on Rule 12(b)(6)
State-law lessons: high bar to third-party beneficiary status under Illinois law; essential terms and mutual assent are indispensable for implied contracts under New York law
Practical implications: media use of purchased personalized content for commentary; deceptive acquisition alone will not defeat fair use absent market substitution or other factors
